1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4.background: Developed by Aron Nimzowitsch, who introduced it to master-level play in the early twentieth century. Every world champion since Capablanca has played it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3.strategy: The flexible main plan: the pawn supports the centre and opens the way for the king's bishop to help control e4. White develops first and does not decide yet how to meet the threat to double the pawns, which leaves a sound, patient game for both sides.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Rubinstein System
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3.background: Named after Akiba Rubinstein. Svetozar Gligorić and Lajos Portisch contributed greatly to its theory and practice at top level during their careers.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2.strategy: Defends the knight and e4 in one move, so ...Bxc3+ can be met by Qxc3 and White keeps the bishop pair and an undamaged pawn structure. The price is time: the queen has moved early and the kingside pieces wait, so Black looks to open the game quickly and use the lead in development.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Classical Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2.background: Also called the Capablanca Variation, it was popular in the early days of the Nimzo-Indian and was eventually superseded by 4.e3. It was revived in the 1990s and is now about as popular as that move.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.g3.strategy: Answers the pin with a slow build-up: the king's bishop will fight for the central light squares from a distance instead of White occupying the centre with pawns. White accepts doubled pawns if Black takes on c3, and a quick strike in the centre by Black is the way to meet the plan.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.g3.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Romanishin Variation

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops a piece and keeps every set-up open: White neither provokes the bishop nor commits a pawn, and waits to see how Black means to fight for e4. It also leaves Black to choose between staying in the pin game and a more classical centre.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Three Knights Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3.background: Also known as the Kasparov Variation, after Garry Kasparov, who used it to great effect against Anatoly Karpov in their 1985 World Championship match, playing it six times for three wins and three draws.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.a3.strategy: Questions the bishop at once: White spends a tempo and accepts doubled c-pawns to get the bishop pair and a broad centre. It is the critical test of Black's plan, since the doubled pawns are either a lasting target or the fuel for a strong pawn centre.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.a3.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Sämisch Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.a3.background: Named after Fritz Sämisch. Mikhail Botvinnik played it five times against Tal in the 1960 World Championship match, all drawn, and once in the 1961 rematch, a win for White. It is rarely seen nowadays.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bg5.strategy: Matches pin for pin: the bishop ties the f6 knight to the queen, so e4 stays out of reach for both sides and Black's knight no longer guards d5. That makes a space-gaining central pawn advance the natural follow-up, at the cost of leaving the pin on c3 in place.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bg5.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Leningrad Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bg5.background: Received its name because its theory was developed extensively by players from Leningrad, such as Boris Spassky.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.f3.strategy: Takes control of e4 with a pawn, so the pinned knight no longer matters and White can build a broad centre. The price is time: the pawn takes the natural square from the g1 knight, and the kingside pieces wait while Black develops.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.f3.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Kmoch Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.f3.background: It has no generally accepted name. Florin Gheorghiu played it often early in his career, and Gligorić named it after him; Alexei Shirov used it with great success in the early 1990s before abandoning it after losing three games in a row with it. It is also called the Kmoch Variation.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qd3.strategy: Defends the knight and the e4 square at once, so White can meet ...Bxc3+ with Qxc3 and keep the structure intact. The queen blocks the natural square of the king's bishop and stands exposed in the centre, which is why it stays a rare choice.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qd3.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Mikenas Attack
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qd3.background: Named after Vladas Mikėnas, and rarely seen.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qb3.strategy: Attacks the undefended bishop and defends the knight, so ...Bxc3+ can be met by Qxc3 and White keeps the bishop pair with an intact structure. But from b3 the queen does nothing about e4, and Black can use that square.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qb3.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Spielmann Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qb3.background: Named after Rudolf Spielmann, who played it at Carlsbad 1929. It was played at master level in the early 1930s but was soon eclipsed in popularity by 4.Qc2, and it remains uncommon despite occasional revivals by Akopian, Malaniuk and Piket.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e4.strategy: A gambit that tries to build the full centre at once, but the pinned knight cannot recapture, so Black simply takes the pawn on e4. The pressure White gets in return does not make up for it.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e4.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Dilworth Gambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e4.background: Named after Vernon Dilworth, who contributed an article on the variation to the March 1949 issue of CHESS magazine.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.a3 Bxc3+.strategy: Cashes in the pin at once: the bishop is given up for the knight so that White's pawns are doubled on the c-file, a lasting weakness. Retreating instead would waste the move, because White would then build the centre with e4 for free.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bg5 h6.strategy: Puts the question to the bishop at once and makes room for the king. If White gives up the bishop for the knight and Black recaptures with the queen, Black gets two bishops against bishop and knight, so White has to keep the tension.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 O-O.strategy: The most common reply: Black castles, a move it will want in any case, and keeps the structure open. Black waits to see where White puts the bishop and knights before deciding between a central pawn strike and taking on c3.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 c5.strategy: Presses on d4 immediately and keeps the central pawn set-up flexible. The threat to double White's pawns is held in reserve, so White has time to arrange to recapture with a piece, at the cost of a less natural development.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 b6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop to tighten the grip on e4, in the spirit of the whole defence: the knight, the pin and the long diagonal all aim at that square. Black delays castling and the central pawns, so White gets time to choose a set-up.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 Nc6.strategy: Develops the queenside knight to prepare a pawn on e5 instead of waiting. The knight blocks the c-pawn, so the pressure on d4 now comes from a piece, and Black gives up some of the usual flexibility for an early fight over the centre.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 Nc6.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Rubinstein System, Taimanov Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 Nc6.background: Named after Mark Taimanov. The young Bobby Fischer tried it several times, and Nukhim Rashkovsky has long favoured it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3 Ne4.strategy: Puts the knight on the central outpost at once to challenge the c3 knight, but Qc2 attacks it while guarding c3, so Black soon has to trade or retreat. White is left with a free hand in the centre, and Black has spent two moves with the same knight.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.f3 d5.strategy: Takes e4 out of White's reach: the d-pawn and the f6 knight both control it, so f3 has bought nothing for the centre. The pawn move has weakened White's kingside and delayed development, while Black fights for the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3 c5.strategy: Attacks d4 at once and keeps the pin on c3, so Black's plan stays clear whatever set-up White chooses. White must decide how to meet the pressure on d4: with a solid pawn on e3 or with a fianchetto.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3 b6.strategy: Aims for a bishop on b7 to control e4 while the bishop on b4 keeps the pin. Black combines the pin with a queenside fianchetto and leaves the pawn centre for later.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3 Bxc3+.strategy: Gives up the bishop before White has spent a move on a3, leaving White the bishop pair and doubled c-pawns. Playable, since the knight is already on f3, but Black has settled the matter unforced and has to prove that the structure outweighs the bishops.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qb3 c5.strategy: The natural counter: the queen attacks the bishop on b4 but does not guard e4, and the pawn both defends the bishop and strikes at d4. Black exploits the poor placement of the queen, and White must decide how to deal with the tension.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 O-O.strategy: The most common reply: Black puts the king away and keeps every plan open. The queen on c2 has made sure White will not get doubled pawns, so Black does not hurry to give up the bishop and waits to see how White commits.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 Nc6.strategy: Attacks the d4 pawn and prepares a pawn centre on d6 and e5 that leaves the other bishop free. The dark-squared bishop is given up, and the knight blocks Black's own c-pawn, which is why the move is rarer today.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 d5.strategy: Stakes a claim in the centre at once and attacks the c4 pawn, which the queen cannot defend because the knight on c3 is in the way. White has to decide immediately how to resolve the central tension.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 c5.strategy: Strikes at the d4 pawn, which the queen on c2 no longer guards. If White defends it, Black keeps the pressure and gets an easy game, so White almost always takes, and Black then plans to win the pawn back.
